outcome: No exact count, and no sourced estimate, of 9x9 Sudoku puzzles with exactly one solution has been published in any source I could find dated after 26 January 2024; the only post-2024 items are two July 2026 arXiv preprints that count grids and clue sets rather than puzzles, plus an unsourced blog figure of about 3 x 10^37 labelled 'Estimated, not exact'.
problem_asks: Single part: the number of 9x9 Sudoku puzzles (partially filled grids with digits 1-9 placed in some cells) that have exactly one completion. The question is 'how many', so the answer is a count of that set, not a bound or an order of magnitude. The statement does not say (a) whether puzzles are counted as labelled placements on the 81 cells or up to symmetry and digit relabelling, or (b) whether a puzzle must be a valid Sudoku in the sense of having a grid completion (it must, to have exactly one). The parent bullet is 'Sudoku:' and the sibling bullets ask how many uniquely solvable puzzles are minimal and what is the maximum number of givens for a minimal puzzle; neither is this question, though a minimal puzzle is always uniquely solvable, so the minimal count is a subset of this one.

events.what_happened: Agnes Herzberg and M. Ram Murty, 'Sudoku Squares and Chromatic Polynomials', Notices of the AMS 54(6), pp. 708-717 (issue dated June/July 2007). Models a puzzle as a partial proper colouring of a graph on the 81 cells, so counting completions becomes evaluating a chromatic-type polynomial, and a value of 1 means exactly one solution. Proves that at least eight of the nine digits must appear as givens for uniqueness. Poses as open: under what conditions a partial colouring extends to a unique proper colouring. The AMS PDF returned HTTP 403, so the content here comes from search snippets of secondary coverage (ScienceDaily dated 8 June 2007; Queen's Mathematical Communicator Spring 2008, which I could not read) and has not been checked against the article.
events.delivers: A framework and a necessary condition, not a count: counting completions reduces to evaluating a polynomial, and uniqueness requires at least eight given digits. It gives no number of uniquely completable puzzles and does not characterise when a partial colouring extends uniquely.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. No count of puzzles with exactly one solution is given, and the open extension question it poses is not resolved in anything I found.
events.time_since_posted: about 19 years; no later digestion or citation found in my searches
events.direction: Neither confirms nor refutes any count; supplies a method and a necessary condition on the number of givens.
sources: https://www.ams.org/notices/200706/tx070600708p.pdf (not opened: HTTP 403; content from search snippets only)

events.what_happened: Bertram Felgenhauer and Frazer Jarvis, brute-force enumeration of completed 9x9 Sudoku grids, giving 6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960. Wikipedia's 'Mathematics of Sudoku' (opened) states this as the number of filled grids and attributes the enumeration to the literature it cites (Lin 2004; OEIS A107739). The Felgenhauer-Jarvis write-up itself was not opened. Secondary search snippets describe it as an 'Enumerating possible Sudoku grids' preprint dated June 2005 (a Scribd copy) and a Mathematical Spectrum 39(1), 2006 version (the journal entry was not verified). A Cornell page dates the method to early 2006 (snippet only). Priority for a complete count is disputed; see disputes.
events.revisions: Preprint 2005 and journal version 2006 per secondary reports, not verified against either.
events.delivers: The number of complete 9x9 grids (no clues). This counts grids, not puzzles, so it does not bear on how many clue sets have exactly one completion.
events.direction: Counts a different object (complete grids); cuts neither way on the puzzle count.

events.what_happened: Count of essentially different completed 9x9 grids under the validity-preserving transformations: 5,472,730,538. Wikipedia's 'Mathematics of Sudoku' (opened) cites Russell and Jarvis (2005 and 2006) for it. The primary Russell-Jarvis material was not opened; the venue is not verified.
events.delivers: A count of grid classes up to symmetry. It counts grids, not puzzles, so it does not bear on the number of uniquely completable puzzles.
events.direction: Counts grid classes under symmetry; cuts neither way on the puzzle count.

events.what_happened: Gary McGuire, Bastian Tugemann and Gilles Civario, 'There is no 16-Clue Sudoku: Solving the Sudoku Minimum Number of Clues Problem', arXiv:1201.0749, first submitted 1 January 2012 (abstract page opened; the PDF was unreadable through my tools). An exhaustive computer search, using a new algorithm for enumerating hitting sets, finds no 16-clue 9x9 puzzle with a unique solution, so 17 is the minimum number of givens. The Nature news item of 6 January 2012 (opened) reports the computation at about 7 million CPU hours. The journal is Experimental Mathematics 23(2), 2014, per the year given in Wikipedia's reference list (opened) and a secondary citation (volume and page not verified). The result is a non-existence statement about a size threshold; it counts nothing.
events.revisions: v1 1 Jan 2012 (shorter title, 43 pages per listing); v2 revised 1 Sep 2013 with the title 'Solving the Sudoku Minimum Number of Clues Problem via Hitting Set Enumeration'; journal version Experimental Mathematics 2014 per Wikipedia reference and secondary citation.
events.delivers: Settles the sibling bullet on the minimum number of givens: no 9x9 puzzle with 16 givens has a unique solution. It establishes nothing about how many puzzles have exactly one solution.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (year 2014 per Wikipedia reference [31]; volume 23(2) pp. 190-217 per a secondary citation, not verified)
checked_by.where: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_of_Sudoku (reference year only; journal page not opened)

checked_by.what_they_did: Reported as seeing the work as 'probably valid' with 'cautious optimism' (Scientific American, 6 Jan 2012); Nature: 'likely valid'

events.direction: Non-existence: no 16-given 9x9 puzzle is uniquely solvable. It cuts against 16-clue uniqueness and says nothing about the count of puzzles.
events.object: No object is exhibited: the result is an exhaustive search showing that no 16-clue puzzle with a unique solution exists. Examples of 17-clue puzzles with a unique solution are known; Wikipedia's Sudoku article (opened) states that tens of thousands of distinct 17-clue puzzles are known.

ai.disclosed_cost: About 7 million CPU hours per Nature (6 Jan 2012); the arXiv PDF was unreadable, so the computing description in the body is not verified.

events.what_happened: Gennesaret Tjusila, Mathieu Besancon, Mark Turner and Thorsten Koch, 'How Many Clues To Give? A Bilevel Formulation For The Minimum Sudoku Clue Problem', arXiv:2305.01697, submitted 2 May 2023 (abstract and HTML opened). For a given completed grid, finds the fewest clues whose unique solution is that grid. Formulated as a binary bilevel program; 50 instances, 95% solved to optimality with a general bilevel solver. The abstract restates that any 9x9 Sudoku puzzle needs at least 17 clues for a unique solution. The arXiv HTML prints no journal reference ('A Preprint'); a ZIB repository listing (search snippet, not opened) gives Operations Research Letters, 2024.
events.revisions: v1 2 May 2023 only seen; later journal version (Operations Research Letters, 2024) per ZIB listing, not verified.
events.delivers: A per-grid minimum-clue computation for 50 instances. It is not a count of puzzles, and it does not bear on the total number of uniquely completable puzzles.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the journal version in 2024 per ZIB repository listing; not verified against the journal

events.direction: Neither way on the count: a per-grid optimisation result.

events.what_happened: Denis Berthier, 'Unbiased Statistics of a CSP - A Controlled-Bias Generator', arXiv:1111.4083, first submitted 17 November 2011 (abstract opened; journal reference given as Innovations in Computing Sciences and Software Engineering (2010) 165-170). The paper restricts its analysis to Sudoku. Search snippets from arXiv:1111.4083 and from Berthier's 'Pattern-Based Constraint Satisfaction and Logic Puzzles', arXiv:1304.1628, first submitted 5 April 2013, report a table giving about 4.6655 x 10^15 minimal puzzles per completed grid with relative error 0.065%, and a total of about 3.1055 x 10^37 minimal 9x9 puzzles, and about 2.5477 x 10^25 non-isomorphic ones. Wikipedia's 'Mathematics of Sudoku' (opened) gives 3.10 x 10^37 minimal puzzles, citing Berthier (2009). I could not read the body of either arXiv paper, and neither abstract I opened contains the number, so the location of the figure and its method are NOT verified by me.
events.revisions: 1111.4083 v1 17 Nov 2011 (only version seen); 1304.1628 v1 5 Apr 2013 (abstract page). Wikipedia cites 2009 and the proceedings are dated 2010, so the first written appearance of the figure may predate the arXiv date; not resolved.
events.delivers: A statistical estimate of the number of minimal 9x9 puzzles (no clue removable without losing uniqueness), about 3.1 x 10^37 with a stated relative error of 0.065%. Minimal puzzles are a subset of uniquely completable puzzles, so if the estimate is right the total in problem_asks is at least about 3.1 x 10^37. The estimate is not an exact count and does not count the total.
events.remains: The total count itself: the figure covers only the minimal subset, which is the sibling bullet, and it is an estimate.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 years; cited by Wikipedia's 'Mathematics of Sudoku' but I found no independent verification
events.doubts: (1) It is a statistical estimate from a generator, and the 0.065% figure is described in a snippet as a one-standard-deviation error, not a bound. (2) Internal arithmetic, from snippet figures only: 4.6655 x 10^15 per grid times 6.6709 x 10^21 grids is about 3.1126 x 10^37, about 0.2% above the stated 3.1055 x 10^37, which is more than the stated 0.065%. This may be a transcription error in the snippet, but I could not check it against the body. (3) The location, date and method of the number are unresolved between the 2011 arXiv paper, the 2013 arXiv paper and Wikipedia's 2009 citation.
events.direction: An estimate of a subset (minimal puzzles). It points to a large count, not to a resolution of the total.

events.what_happened: Blog post 'How Many Sudokus Are There?' on thesudoku.com, byline Mark Citizen, dated 31 March 2026 from the URL (the date does not appear in the body). Its 'What We're Counting' table gives 'Puzzles with unique solutions' as about 3 x 10^37, with the note 'Estimated, not exact'. The post says an exact count 'is considered computationally intractable with current methods'. It cites no source or method for the puzzle row. It labels the grid count 'Exact, computed 2005'.
events.delivers: An unsourced magnitude, about 3 x 10^37, for the total in problem_asks, labelled as an estimate. It establishes no count and gives no method.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The figure has no stated basis, so the post does not settle any part of it.
events.doubts: The row cites no source. Its magnitude matches the minimal-puzzle estimate of about 3.1 x 10^37 (Berthier), which is the same number rounded to one significant figure, so it may be that figure relabelled as a total. The post does not say. If the minimal estimate is right, a total equal to 3 x 10^37 would be too small, but the rounded '~3' cannot distinguish a total of 3.0 x 10^37 from 3.1 x 10^37.
events.direction: A magnitude for the total, with no direction relative to any claim.

events.what_happened: Fernanda Pereira, 'Counting, Symmetries and Equivalence Classes of Sudoku Grids', arXiv:2607.20669, math.GM (MSC 05E18; 05A18, 05B15), single author, no affiliation listed, 24 pages, 3 tables. Recovers the 44 isomorphism classes of first-band column-partition configurations, a step in the earlier grid enumeration, by treating them as unordered triples of column partitions up to relabelling and applying Burnside's lemma by hand, with ancillary Python verification scripts. Mentions the 5,472,730,538 essentially different grids as older work. It counts complete grids and their equivalence classes, not puzzles.
events.revisions: v1 submitted 22 Jul 2026; v2 revised 24 Jul 2026 (content of v2 not examined).
events.delivers: Re-derives an intermediate count (44 first-band classes) of complete grids by a Burnside argument. It counts grids and symmetry classes of grids, not puzzles with exactly one completion, so it is outside this bullet's scope.
events.directly_checkable: The 44-class and 5,472,730,538 figures can be checked against the ancillary verification scripts named in the paper (verification_burnside_44.py, verification_section3.py), per the arXiv listing; not run by me.
events.direction: Re-derives an existing intermediate count by a different method. It does not move any count of puzzles.

systems.name: Claude Sonnet 5 model, accessed via claude.ai
systems.what_it_did: Per the author: language editing and translation; 'assistance in deriving and developing some of the mathematical arguments'; writing the Python scripts used in the computational verifications. The paper does not say which mathematical arguments, so it is not established whether the Burnside derivation of the 44 classes, or any other result, depends on the model. The author states they reviewed, verified and complemented all such content and checked all computations and claims.
systems.basis_quote: While preparing this work, the author used the artificial intelligence assistant Claude (Claude Sonnet 5 model, accessed via claude.ai) for language editing and translation, for assistance in deriving and developing some of the mathematical arguments, and for writing the Python scripts used in the computational verifications described throughout the paper.

events.what_happened: David Eppstein and Xinyu (Cindy) Zhang, 'Sudoku Grids That Require Many Clues', arXiv:2607.05728, submitted 7 July 2026, cs.DM and cs.DS, 2 pages, 'to appear at 28th Japan Conference on Discrete and Computational Geometry, Graphs, and Games, Tokyo, 2026' (the arXiv comment; Eppstein's publications page gives 26th, and the conference site was not opened). Shows that most filled n^2 x n^2 grids need all but a logarithmic fraction of cells as clues, and constructs 9x9 grids needing 18 clues and 16x16 grids needing 80 clues by packing independent Latin squares. Motivated by worst-case solving time; gives a 2^{O(n^4/log n)} average-case bound. The paper concerns the clues that determine a specified grid, not the number of puzzles with exactly one solution.
events.delivers: For specified filled grids, the minimum number of clues that determines the grid. It gives an 18-clue 9x9 example, and a 16x16 example needing 80 clues. It does not count puzzles with exactly one solution.

checked_by.qualification: Conference programme for a refereed-style discrete geometry and graph meeting (review process not verified)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for presentation per the arXiv comment; the conference page was not opened

events.directly_checkable: The 9x9 example needing 18 clues is an explicit grid that can be checked by a solver; the paper's construction was not checked by me.
events.direction: Concerns minimum clue counts for particular grids; it does not count puzzles and does not change the total.
events.object: Explicit constructions: a family of 9x9 grids whose minimal clue set has 18 elements, and a 16x16 grid needing 80 clues, both built by packing independent Latin squares. Explicit, not existence-only, per the abstract.

disputes.summary: Priority for the complete count of 9x9 grids. Secondary reports say Guenter Stertenbrink ('QSCGZ') posted a complete enumeration to rec.puzzles in September 2003, and Felgenhauer and Jarvis confirmed it in 2005. Other reports say the 2005 result was the first. Not resolved; it concerns grids, not puzzles.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_of_Sudoku (opened; gives 2005 and 2006 for Russell and Jarvis, not the 2003 posting)

disputes.summary: The figure of about 3 x 10^37 is labelled 'puzzles with unique solutions' by the 2026 blog (estimated, unsourced) but is the magnitude of Wikipedia's and Berthier's estimate for minimal puzzles (3.10 x 10^37, 'not precisely known'). Minimal puzzles are a subset of uniquely completable puzzles, so the two are different quantities even though they match in magnitude.

The date of the minimal-puzzle estimate is not fixed. Wikipedia cites Berthier (2009); the arXiv copy is dated 17 November 2011; the proceedings volume is dated 2010 (journal reference on the arXiv abstract page).

summary: The bullet is the first of three sub-bullets under 'Sudoku' on the Wikipedia list (the other two ask how many uniquely solvable puzzles are minimal and the maximum number of givens for a minimal puzzle), so it asks for the total count of 9x9 puzzles with exactly one completion, not the minimal subset. I found no exact count and no sourced estimate of that total in any source dated after 26 January 2024. The post-2024 items are two July 2026 arXiv preprints, neither of which counts puzzles. Pereira (arXiv:2607.20669, submitted 22 Jul 2026) counts complete grids and their symmetry classes. Her AI-use statement credits 'Claude Sonnet 5 model, accessed via claude.ai' with 'assistance in deriving and developing some of the mathematical arguments' but does not say which arguments; whether the hand Burnside derivation of the 44 first-band classes is among them is my inference, not something the paper says. Eppstein and Zhang (arXiv:2607.05728, submitted 7 Jul 2026) give the clue counts needed to determine particular grids (18 for some 9x9 grids) and disclose no AI use. Earlier events are all outside this bullet's scope: Herzberg and Murty's 2007 polynomial reformulation with an open question about unique extension (the Notices PDF was unreachable, so this rests on secondary snippets), the Felgenhauer-Jarvis 2005 grid count, the Russell-Jarvis symmetry classes, McGuire, Tugemann and Civario's 2012 proof that no 16-clue puzzle is uniquely solvable (which settles the sibling minimum-givens bullet and is the only one of these that was published in a journal and received press comment), Tjusila et al.'s 2023 per-grid minimum-clue computation, and Berthier's estimate of the minimal-puzzle count. Berthier is the one quantitative item that bears on the total, and only indirectly: every minimal puzzle is uniquely solvable, so if the estimate is right the total is at least about 3.1 x 10^37. I could not confirm the number from the body of either Berthier paper (the arXiv PDFs were unreadable through my tools, and the abstracts I opened do not contain it), so its location rests on search snippets and Wikipedia's citation. Its own snippet figures do not reproduce the stated total within the stated error (4.6655 x 10^15 per grid times 6.6709 x 10^21 grids is about 3.1126 x 10^37, not 3.1055 x 10^37). The Wikipedia 'Mathematics of Sudoku' article calls the minimal count 'not precisely known' and states no total. The only total in circulation is a commercial blog (Mark Citizen, 31 March 2026) that lists about 3 x 10^37 as 'Estimated, not exact' with no source or method, and says an exact count is computationally intractable with current methods (also unsourced). That figure may be the minimal estimate relabelled, but a rounded '3' cannot show it. On human checking, no post-2024 item has a named qualified person checking it in public. For the 2012 McGuire result, unnamed mathematicians at a Boston conference were quoted as finding it 'probably valid' (Scientific American, 6 January 2012), and no formal machine check was found. On AI, the only system named in any item near this bullet is Claude in the Pereira preprint, which concerns grid counting. A separate August 2026 preprint by Padhi (arXiv:2608.11290) credits Claude but treats five other enumerative combinatorics problems and does not mention Sudoku, so I did not record it as an event.
competing_reading: The question could be read as already answered to within an error bar. Wikipedia presents Berthier's 3.10 x 10^37 as the count for minimal puzzles, and the 2026 blog presents about 3 x 10^37 as the count for all unique-solution puzzles. A reader who takes either as the state of knowledge would call the bullet 'estimated', not 'open'. Against that: the Wikipedia article itself says the minimal count is 'not precisely known', the blog gives no source, and the Berthier figure is for a subset and is not reproduced by its own snippet arithmetic. On AI, a reader who takes Pereira's 'assistance in deriving ... some of the mathematical arguments' at face value could say the model contributed to the grid-count derivation. That would be an AI contribution to a grid-count result, which is outside this bullet's scope.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The body text of arXiv:1111.4083 or arXiv:1304.1628, or the 2010 CISSE proceedings, showing the 3.1055 x 10^37 figure, its method, its date and whether it counts minimal or all uniquely completable puzzles. (2) An exact count of uniquely completable 9x9 puzzles, or a published bound with its method, which is the only thing that would answer this bullet. (3) The Herzberg and Murty Notices text, the Felgenhauer and Jarvis paper, and the Queen's newsletter, none of which I could read. (4) For the AI question on Pereira, the author's statement of which arguments the model helped develop; this would not change the scope finding, which is that the paper does not count puzzles.
